answer:
Among the 35 Psychology studies in the Reproducibility Project Psychology subset (project == 'rpp') that were successfully replicated (replicated == 1), 16 in 35 — approximately 45.7% — had a junior professor (most senior replication author with seniority.r = Assistant Professor or Assistant, excluding Researcher). If 'junior professor' is restricted to Assistant Professor only, the proportion is 10/35 = 28.6%. The estimate is robust: the full rpp sample (n=97) gives 38/97 = 39.2%, and excluding the 7 drop-flagged rows (n=31) gives 16/31 = 51.6% (so ~46–52% under the primary junior-definition).

Workflow: load the main study dataset (927 O/R pairs, unique ids); restrict to project=='rpp' (97 rows) with complete seniority and replicated fields (no missing, no duplicate ids); use the provided `replicated` flag as authoritative (a recomputed p<=0.05-same-direction rule gives 33 vs 35, documented as a 2-row discrepancy); compute the proportion of replicated==1 rows (n=35) whose seniority.r is in {Assistant Professor, Assistant}; report Assistant-Professor-only and all-rpp / drop-excluded readings as sensitivity.
